newsitem.title: USA: EU official sees breakthrough in U.S. meat talks.
newsitem.headline: EU official sees breakthrough in U.S. meat talks.

text.p: A senior European Union official said Wednesday there was an "important breakthrough" in talks this week with the United States on EU and U.S. meat import regulations and said an agreement by April 1 looks very likely.
"We are both sides dedicated to reaching an agreement ... there is nothing coming out of the last two days that makes me think it is not possible," said Lars Hoelgaard, who headed the EU delegation.
Hoelgaard briefed reporters after two days of talks with Agriculture Department officials on a so-called Veterinary Equivalency agreement.
Hoelgaard said another set of negotiations is planned for the week of February 24, and that he expects a full week of talks at that time to resolve remaining differences.
Hoelgaard said the USDA has agreed to accept Europe's regionalization system in dealing with disease outbreaks in animals. This has been a major sticking point in the talks.

Under Europe's regionalization system, if there is an animal health problem in a certain region of a country, the EU zones off the area and implements measures to restrict into or out of the affected area. There can be movement into or out of non-affected areas of the country.
The United States has refused to recognize Europe's system, however, and has banned meat imports from entire nation if a problem has been cited in any part of the country.

Hoelgaard said the U.S. "country by country" approach has "somewhat of an illogical approach," and that the EU position has been that "what can trade freely within the Community can trade freely with the United States."
According to Hoelgaard, this week the U.S. side determined that the Agriculture Secretary has the power to recognize Europe's regionalization scheme, removing a major obstacle in the talks.
